title: The Odd Women: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: A Woman's Right to Work: Setting the Stakes

utterances.text: Welcome to The Odd Women Unpacked, a close reading of George Gissing's fierce, funny, and quietly devastating novel of 1893.
Over the course of this series, we're going to read the novel with the attention it deserves — pulling apart its arguments, its characters, its surprising comedy, and its moments of real anguish.
Gissing published The Odd Women at a moment when the so-called Woman Question was not an abstraction but a daily crisis for hundreds of thousands of women without income, prospects, or protection.
His title comes from the statistical surplus — more women than men in Victorian England — and he uses it to ask what those surplus lives are actually worth.
Joining me today are three guests whose disagreements are at least as interesting as their agreements.

Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more classic audiobooks than almost anyone alive, and he comes to Gissing as a performer first — listening for the rhythms, the comedy, the moments written for the voice.

Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads novels as stories about individual character under moral pressure — and who will, I suspect, resist any reading that turns Gissing into a pamphleteer.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every novel as an anatomy of class power, and who believes the most radical novelists are often more radical than they themselves knew.
Let's begin with the question the novel poses from almost its first pages: what is a woman's right to work, and who gets to define it?
What strikes me immediately, coming to this novel fresh — or fresh-ish, I've done it twice in the booth — is how much Gissing trusts his heroine's voice.
Rhoda Nunn is not a mouthpiece. She's a character who argues badly sometimes, loses her temper, contradicts herself.
And yet the things she believes in — her actual convictions — are stated with such compact, almost epigrammatic force.
There's a moment when she's pressed on the subject of marriage — she's asked to account for it, to justify her position — and she simply refuses to engage on those terms.
One mustn't undertake too much — that line is devastating in performance.
It's so dry. So perfectly placed. It sounds almost modest, but it is the opposite of modest.
Oliver is quite right that the line is well-placed. But I want to register a mild dissent about what we should make of it.
Rhoda Nunn is a woman of powerful will and genuine intelligence. These are, in the novel, her great virtues.
But there is a rigidity in her thinking — a refusal to allow the particular case to complicate the general principle — that Gissing observes with a slightly cooler eye than his admirers allow.
Consider the quarrel with Mary Barfoot — this wonderful, crackling exchange where Rhoda refuses the emotional argument entirely.
Now, Rhoda believes she is speaking on the side of reason. And in a narrow logical sense, she is.
But Gissing lets us see that this very certainty — this immunity to personal feeling — is also a kind of limitation of sympathy.
I hear Edmund's point, but I think framing Rhoda's position as a limitation rather misses what Gissing is anatomising.
The pressure on women in this novel to be emotionally accommodating — to make personal feeling the supreme criterion — is itself a form of social control.
When Rhoda insists that movements for change cannot be governed by personal attachment, she is refusing a trap — the trap of sentimentality that keeps women in their place.
And then there's the passage where she articulates the affirmative case — not just what she refuses, but what she is building.
That phrase — weariness and lamentation — is exactly the script that Victorian ideology handed to single women.
Rhoda is refusing to perform that script. And Gissing, I'd argue, is fully on her side in that refusal.
Daniel's reading of that passage is entirely convincing, and I want to add something about the texture of how Gissing writes Rhoda's sense of purpose.
There's another moment — earlier in the novel — where she describes the 'odd women' themselves, this surplus population, in terms that are almost exhilarating.
A great reserve. I love that. It's military language, almost — these women as a standing army waiting to be deployed.
And there's something thrilling about hearing a Victorian heroine claim that language for women's work rather than men's wars.
The language of reserves and substitutes is interesting precisely because it is impersonal. These are women as a category, not as individuals.
And that, I think, is where one ought to pause. Gissing is a great novelist partly because he notices the cost of programmes as well as their necessity.
Rhoda's formulation — train the reserve — has a bracing clarity. But it also, if one listens carefully, treats individual women as instruments of a larger design.
The question the novel will go on to explore — with some discomfort — is whether Rhoda herself can survive the logic of her own position.
Edmund raises a real tension, and I don't want to simply dissolve it. The novel does hold Rhoda to account for her abstractions.
But I'd insist that the structural conditions producing those abstractions — the sheer material desperation of women without income or training — are the prior fact.
Rhoda's project isn't ideology for its own sake. It's a response to a system that has already reduced women to instruments — of marriage, of domestic labour, of male convenience.
What Gissing gives us, uniquely, is a heroine who has diagnosed that system and is attempting — however imperfectly — to build something outside it.
That phrase — building something outside the system — feels like exactly the right place to pause before we move forward.
Because the novel isn't only about the women who refuse the old terms — it's also about the men and women who are very much inside them.
Coming up: we turn to Gissing's gallery of courtship — the rituals, the negotiations, the comic and occasionally painful machinery of Victorian romantic pursuit.

segments.title: The Comedy of Courtship and Constraint

utterances.text: We've been talking about what work means for women in this novel — the dignity and the danger of it.
But Gissing is also, quietly and devastatingly, a comic novelist of marriage — and that's where we turn now.
I want to start with Barfoot's friend Poppleton, because Gissing absolutely earns his laughter there.
Barfoot is describing the marriage — this poor, well-meaning man trapped with a woman who cannot follow a joke.
And Gissing gives us the full, torturous scene — the unbeautiful little parlour, the social dread, the perspiration on the forehead.
The passage builds to something I could read aloud every week for the rest of my life.
"Poor old Poppleton! Again and again I have heard him — what do you think? — laboriously explaining jests to her."
"I have known him explain, and re-explain, for a quarter of an hour, and invariably without success."
That word — laboriously — is everything.
The heroic, futile labour of the well-intentioned man.
It is genuinely very funny — Gissing at his most Dickensian, I'd say.
But I think the comedy rests on something more than incompatibility of wit.
It is a scene about a man's irreducible loneliness inside a marriage — the wall she stares at is exactly right.
Gissing doesn't blame Mrs. Poppleton, notice — she is simply opaque, not wicked.
The tragedy is structural — two people joined by convention with nothing to share.
Which is precisely why Gissing insists, in the Widdowson marriage, on showing us the architecture of control before the walls come down.
The Poppleton scene is brilliant, but I'd argue it functions as a kind of warning Gissing places in Barfoot's mouth.
Barfoot tells the story to excuse his own refusal to marry — it's a self-serving parable.
Meanwhile, Monica has no equivalent warning story — she has only the arithmetic of her options.
Gissing shows us her situation with deliberate plainness — she is good-looking, she knows it, and she knows it will not be enough.
"Had she really the least chance of marrying a man whom she could respect — not to say love?"
That question mark is the whole novel in miniature.
Respect first, love second — and even that ranked and cautious aspiration seems barely within reach.
And when Monica does try to conduct herself with any independence — even in courtship — the novel shows how the rules bite immediately.
There's a speech she gives to Widdowson early in their acquaintance that I find quietly remarkable.
"I may perhaps come to feel you as a girl ought to when she marries, and how else can I tell unless I meet you and talk with you?"
"Yet we have gone against the ordinary rule, and people would make us suffer for it — or me, at all events."
That final clause — or me, at all events — is where Gissing slides the knife in.
Monica knows perfectly well who will bear the social cost, and she names it with a composure that is almost heartbreaking.
She speaks with remarkable clarity for a girl in her position — and I mean that as the highest compliment.
She is not a polemical mouthpiece — she is a young woman reasoning through a genuinely painful situation.
And Widdowson, to give him his due, is not a villain at this stage — he is merely a conventional man who has never been required to think.
Gissing is quite precise about this — he tells us Widdowson imagined authority would never be necessary.
"All his fears, after all, were not groundless."
There is something almost Johnsonian in the compression of that sentence — the irony so dry it barely registers as irony at all.
Groundless — but what are these fears exactly?
Monica has done nothing — she simply wants to move about more freely.
And his response is the response of the institution — mild discipline, domestic tasks, the needle as surveillance.
Gissing makes the mechanism absolutely explicit here.
"By way of mild discipline, he first of all suggested a closer attention to the affairs of the house."
Suggested — not ordered.
The soft word makes it worse — the power is most suffocating when it doesn't need to announce itself.
And then comes the religion — which is where Gissing is at his most wickedly funny.
Widdowson is not himself a believer in any serious sense — he has his doubts.
But he would not for any account permit Monica to suspect this.
"Like most men of his kind, he viewed religion as a precious and powerful instrument for directing the female conscience."
Precious and powerful instrument — as though faith were a particularly reliable piece of household equipment.
Barrow's Sermons on Sunday, the needle on Monday — Widdowson is running a whole programme of management.
One shouldn't entirely mock Widdowson for that — the Victorian belief that social order rested on female piety was almost universal.
What Gissing mocks is not the belief itself but the bad faith — the man who doubts privately and enforces publicly.
That hypocrisy is the real target.
And it connects directly to what Gissing says about Widdowson's fundamental conception of women.
There's a passage in chapter twenty-three that I think is the cold theoretical heart of everything we've been describing.
"Women were very like children; it was rather a task to amuse them and to keep them out of mischief."
Gissing calls this the most primitive male conception of the feminine being — and he means it as a clinical diagnosis, not a joke.
Widdowson can update his vocabulary but not his cosmology — woman as child, marriage as containment.
What makes it so perfectly observed is the line immediately after — intimacy with Monica had greatly affected his views, yet chiefly by disturbing them.
He's been shaken, but not enlightened.
The architecture wobbles but the load-bearing walls stay up.
A disturbed but unenlightened man — and a marriage that is starting to crack under the strain of those undisturbed prejudices.
In our next section, we follow that crack as it widens — Widdowson's anxiety tips into something darker and more obsessive, and Gissing maps it with the precision of a case study.
We've been laughing — or at least wincing with recognition — at the comic choreography of courtship in this novel.
But Gissing won't let us stay comfortable for long — and nowhere is that clearer than in the marriage of Monica and Widdowson.
What Gissing gives us in these chapters is something closer to Victorian pathology than Victorian romance.
A man in the grip of jealousy he cannot master, a woman trapped in a union that has curdled into something almost gothic.
Oliver, you've voiced more tormented husbands than most actors alive — how does Widdowson register for you on the page?
What strikes me immediately — as a performer — is the word Gissing chooses for what possesses Widdowson.
Not torment. Not anxiety. "Insufferable misery."
That's a phrase with physical weight — you feel the man buckling under it.
And then Gissing does this extraordinary thing — he reaches into Widdowson's mind and finds something genuinely frightening.
"Terrible thoughts smouldered in his mind; he felt himself to be one of those men who are driven by passion into crime."
"Smouldered" — not blazed, not erupted — smouldered.
That's the word of a man who has learned to live with his own dangerous heat, as one lives with a faulty boiler.
There's almost a terrible self-knowledge in him — which makes him worse, not better.
The self-knowledge is precisely what gives this character his moral weight, I think.
Widdowson is not a villain. He is a weak man — and there is a great tradition in English fiction of taking that distinction seriously.
What I find remarkable is that Gissing grants him the capacity for remorse even as he denies him the capacity for reform.
He sees himself clearly — and then cannot act on what he sees.
And the confession he makes to Monica is devastating in its honesty — and its irreversibility.
"I have my faults; I know them only too well. One of them is that I cannot bear you to make friends with people who are not of my kind."
"I shall never be able to endure that."
"I shall never be able to endure that" — it's almost a lament. He's mourning his own limitation.
I'd push back slightly on the framing of individual weakness — because Widdowson's particular pathology is not free-floating.
When he says he cannot bear Monica associating with people "not of my kind," that is a class statement dressed as a psychological one.
His jealousy is inseparable from his anxiety about social position, about the ownership of a wife who might transgress the boundaries he's mapped onto her.
And watch what happens when Virginia's degradation enters the picture — the logic is nakedly revealing.
"They were sisters; they had characteristics in common, family traits, weaknesses."
"If the elder woman could fall into this degradation, might there not be possibilities in Monica's character such as he had refused to contemplate?"
He's treating women as specimens of a type — biologically interchangeable, constitutionally suspect.
This isn't private neurosis — it's the ideology of the period wearing a husband's face.
Daniel's right about the ideology — but I don't think that lets Gissing off the hook as a dramatist either.
Because look at what Gissing does with the surveillance scenes.
Widdowson walking the pavement outside Mrs. Conisbee's house — in the rain, feverish — with, as Gissing puts it, "a constable's regularity."
And then comes this line — which just stopped me when I first read it.
"A little more than twelve months ago! And he had waited, longed for marriage through half a lifetime."
Twelve months. Half a lifetime of longing, reduced to this — a wet pavement, a locked door, a burning fever.
Gissing doesn't editorialize. He just lines up the numbers and lets the arithmetic do its work.
The pathos there is real — and I think one must resist the temptation to convert it entirely into social critique.
This is a man who has destroyed what he most desired — through an inability he genuinely cannot overcome.
That is a tragedy in the classical sense — hamartia, if one's permitted the Greek.
But the other side of the picture — Monica's side — is equally unsparing.
Gissing is extraordinary in his willingness to render what it feels like to be trapped inside a marriage one has ceased to feel.
"Every day the distance between them widened, and when he took her in his arms she had to struggle with a sense of shrinking, of disgust."
"Shrinking" and then "disgust" — those two words move in a terrible progression.
One is involuntary. The other is a verdict.
And Gissing is explicit about why Monica cannot simply speak this truth — cannot say to Widdowson what she actually feels.
The novel is precise: "The moment such a truth had passed her lips she must leave him."
That's not psychology — that's economics. She has nowhere to go and no means to get there.
Her silence is not weakness — it is rational calculation under conditions of total material dependency.
And the novel makes the parallel explicit — her "dark foresight" of separation mirrors Widdowson's "lurid visions" of violence.
Two people locked in adjacent nightmares, neither able to speak, because the institution of marriage has made speech impossible.
The final image of those chapters is the one that haunts me most as a performer.
When Monica clings to his arms and Gissing describes what her face is actually showing — it's two things at once.
"The bloodless lips, the choked voice, meant dread of him, but the distortion of her features was hatred and the will to resist."
Fear and hatred — simultaneously, in one face.
You cannot stage that line — you can only read it. The novel is doing something the theatre cannot.
Two people in the same room, reading each other's faces — and finding nothing left to hold onto.
What's remarkable is that Gissing renders all of this — the jealousy, the disgust, the calculation — without a single authorial judgment.
Which raises the question of how he does it — the narrative voice, the distance, the control.
That's precisely what we'll turn to next — the architecture of Gissing's narration, and how it holds all of this without breaking.
We've been watching Widdowson's obsessive grip tighten chapter by chapter, and what struck me in our last discussion was how much the narrator is doing to keep us at just the right distance from him.
Which brings us to Gissing's narration itself — the architecture of how he builds and places his characters before us.
The first thing you notice, performing Gissing, is that he is extraordinarily precise about bodies before he's precise about souls.
There's a passage in Chapter Eight where he introduces Everard Barfoot, and it's a masterclass in controlled physical description.
You get the tall frame, the chestnut hair, the full lips — every detail chosen — and then Gissing does this delicious thing.

"From his appearance one would have expected him to speak in rather loud and decided tones; but he had a soft voice, and used it with all the discretion of good breeding, so that at times it seemed to caress the ear."
To caress the ear — Gissing hands you a warning dressed as a compliment.
That voice will be used on women throughout this novel, and Gissing wants us to feel its danger even as we admire it.
Oliver is quite right that it's a warning, but I'd push back gently on calling it a structural device alone.
Gissing's narrator is doing something older and more novelistic — he is drawing character, in the full eighteenth-century sense of the word.
The smile that is "restrained to the expression of a delicate, good-natured irony" — that is not ideology, that is a man being pinned to the page.
And what Gissing pins him to, ultimately, is his own inadequacy — which the narrator diagnoses with devastating precision in Chapter Twenty-Two.
There is a sentence about Bevis — poor, flustered, morally invertebrate Bevis — that I consider one of the finest pieces of characterisation in late Victorian fiction.
"He had not in him the stuff of vigorous rascality, still less the only other quality which can support a man in such a situation as this — heroism of moral revolt."
"So he cut a very poor figure, and was dolefully aware of it."
That is the whole moral diagnosis — vigorous villain or moral hero, and Bevis is capable of neither.
The narrator does not rage at him — he simply measures him, and finds him short.
I want to stay with that passage a moment, because what Edmund is calling moral diagnosis I'd call social anatomy.
Bevis is not merely a weak individual — he is a certain kind of middle-class Englishman produced by a certain kind of social formation.
The novel tells us he was "timorously selfish from the first" — timorous selfishness is not a moral failing, it is a class posture.
A man raised to expect comfort, to avoid exposure, to retreat behind "tinsel phrases" when reality becomes inconvenient.
And who bears the cost of his timidity? Monica does. Monica, who is trapped, who has nowhere to go.
And Gissing signals all of this through the narrator's tone — which is precisely, mercilessly comic.
"He talked, talked" — that repetition is musical, almost contemptuous.
The narrator mimics Bevis's own feebleness in the rhythm of the sentence, and you feel it in your mouth when you read it aloud.
It's the kind of sentence that makes a reader smile and wince simultaneously — which is Gissing at his absolute best.
What I find equally remarkable is the narrator's relationship to Mary Barfoot — which is quite different in register.
When Gissing narrates through Mary's consciousness, the prose becomes purposeful, polemical, almost oratorical.
She delivers a speech in Chapter Thirteen that Gissing renders without irony — and the absence of irony is itself a narrative choice.
Listen to how she frames her own position:
"I am a troublesome, aggressive, revolutionary person. I want to do away with that common confusion of the words womanly and womanish."
"And I see very clearly that this can only be effected by an armed movement, an invasion by women of the spheres which men have always forbidden us to enter."
That is the narrator lending his full authority to a character's ideology — something Gissing's critics have never quite resolved.
The critics who find it unresolved are perhaps expecting a comfortable distance that Gissing has deliberately refused.
Mary's speech on Ruskin is not decoration — it is the theoretical spine of the whole novel.
She says: "A womanly occupation means, practically, an occupation that a man disdains."
That is an analysis of the labour market, not merely a feminist slogan.
The devaluation of work is inseparable from the devaluation of the people assigned to it — and Gissing, through Mary, names that mechanism precisely.

She even anticipates the counter-argument — the Ruskinian ideal — and disposes of it with magnificent impatience: "Were we living in an ideal world, I think women would not go to sit all day in offices."
"But the fact is that we live in a world as far from ideal as can be conceived."
The narrator isn't standing back from that. He is standing behind it.
And yet the same narrator, only a few chapters later, can step back and observe the whole household drama with this extraordinary tenderness.
There's a passage about Mary Barfoot in Chapter Twenty-One that I find almost impossible not to read with a kind of quiet awe.
Gissing describes her as having outlived what he calls those "fervours of instinct which often make the middle life of an unwedded woman one long repining."
"One long repining" — he doesn't flinch from what that life could have been, even as he celebrates what she's made of it instead.
And then he describes her watching the younger people in her household, calling it "a comedy, a drama, which had power to excite all her disinterested emotions."
A comedy and a drama simultaneously — that double register is the whole novel in miniature.
That phrase — "disinterested emotions" — is doing a great deal of work.
Mary has achieved something that most characters in this novel cannot: the capacity to feel deeply without needing the outcome to serve herself.
Gissing says she has "that ruling intelligence which enabled her to transmute" experience "into principles."
Transmutation of experience into principle — that is what Gissing asks of his narrator too, and what he asks of his reader.
The novel is itself a kind of moral intelligence directed at material that might easily have become mere polemic or mere pathos.
What strikes me across all three of these passages is how much Gissing's narration relies on the specific weight of place and solitude — characters observed not just in argument but in stillness.
Which is exactly what we want to turn to next — the way Gissing uses atmosphere and isolation not as background, but as something the characters must actively reckon with.

segments.title: Isolation and Atmosphere: The Weight of Choice

utterances.text: We've been talking about how Gissing shapes our perception through the architecture of his narration.
But narration doesn't exist in a vacuum — it's embedded in weather, landscape, and the inner atmospheres of desperate minds.
There's a passage early in Chapter Twenty-Five that I keep returning to, because it does something quite remarkable.
Rhoda is on holiday at the seashore — a woman who has built her entire identity around principled self-sufficiency.
And Gissing gives her bad weather. Not metaphorical bad weather — actual stormclouds and mutterings of thunder.
But then simultaneously, without announcement, Monica is fleeing her home in pelting rain — and Gissing merges the two women's crises in a single sentence.
The passage reads as follows.
"On the last night of the week — when Monica fled from her home in pelting rain — tempest broke upon the mountains and the sea."
That parenthetical — Monica's flight tucked inside Rhoda's storm — is not accidental.
Gissing is telling us that these two women are bound together by forces neither of them controls — social, emotional, meteorological.
And what a sentence to read aloud.
"Tempest broke upon the mountains and the sea" — there's a biblical cadence there, almost Lear on the heath.
Gissing knew exactly what he was doing rhythmically — that sentence lands like a gavel.
And then — and this is the detail I love — Rhoda is at her window watching lightning illuminate the crags of Wastwater.
She's sleepless, wakeful until early morning, as the text says.
"Miles of distance were annihilated, and it seemed but a step to those stern crags and precipices."
Annihilated. Stern crags and precipices. That's not the vocabulary of a cosy Victorian holiday novel.
Gissing is reaching for something violent and sublime — because that's what Rhoda's inner life has become.
I wouldn't resist that reading — but I'd want to press on what the landscape is actually dramatising about Rhoda's character.
Because Gissing brings us, in Chapter Twenty-Seven, to something far more disturbing than a storm outside a window.
Rhoda returns from her holiday with sunken cheeks, and she has resolved to betray nothing — not to Miss Barfoot, not to anyone.
Gissing describes her state of mind — and it is worth hearing this precisely.
"Her state of mind resembled that of the ascetic who has arrived at a morbid delight in self-torture."
Now, Daniel will want to read that as ideology — as what the system has done to her.
But I think Gissing is writing about something older and more universal: the will turning against itself when it cannot have what it loves.
That is not a Victorian pathology. That is a human one.
Edmund, I accept the human dimension entirely — but I think you've separated two things Gissing keeps deliberately fused.
Because the very next sentence tells us what Rhoda's will turns against — and it isn't simply Everard.
Gissing writes — and this is the sentence I find most devastating in these chapters —

"She regarded the world with an intense bitterness, and persuaded herself not only that the thought of Everard Barfoot was hateful to her soul, but that sexual love had become, and would ever be, to her an impure idea, a vice of blood."
A vice of blood. Rhoda has internalised the very condemnation the world levels at women who desire.
She began the novel as someone who refused those terms. She ends this chapter having accepted them from the inside.
That is not simply a human story about unrequited love. That is a social mechanism laid bare.
And then there's Monica — who is living the other version of exactly this entrapment.
Chapter Twenty-Nine gives us Monica in the dark, at night, and the prose shifts into something that sounds almost like a confessional.
The passage is extraordinary. Listen to how it builds.
"Reason availed nothing; its exercise seemed criminal. The old faiths, never abandoned, though modified by the breath of intellectual freedom that had just touched her, reasserted all their power."
The breath of intellectual freedom that had just touched her — that phrase alone is worth the price of admission.
Monica has had just enough education to see clearly — and not nearly enough to escape.
And then Gissing delivers the sentence that stops you cold.
"Her soul trembled in its nakedness."
Five words. That's all. And you don't need any more.
That is one of those sentences that justifies the entire novel.
And what gives it such force is the word nakedness — not weakness, not fear, but nakedness.
The soul stripped of all its social defences, its habitual arguments, its borrowed freedoms.
Monica is exposed — not by Gissing's irony, but by her own conscience.
And that is a very different kind of nakedness from the one Daniel describes in Rhoda — an imposed verdict rather than an inner reckoning.
I'd grant that distinction — but Monica's inner reckoning is also shaped from without.
Later in that same chapter, Gissing shows us a different Monica — the one who takes the train to Chelsea.
She walks along the Embankment deliberately, loitering to outrage the proprieties, and Gissing gives us this.
"This semblance of freedom, together with the sense of having taken a courageous resolve, raised her spirits."
Semblance. Gissing doesn't say freedom — he says semblance of freedom.
The word does the entire work of social critique in a single syllable.
Monica can walk along the Embankment and feel brave. But she is still being tracked, still performing her own liberation for an audience that may include a detective.
The tragedy is not that she lacks courage. The tragedy is that courage alone cannot purchase what she needs.
And there's something almost mordantly funny in it too — she hopes a detective is following her.
She wants the surveillance to be real so that she can have the satisfaction of evading it.
Gissing has a very precise understanding of what small rebellions feel like to people trapped in large systems.
Rhoda's morbid asceticism, Monica's trembling soul, that semblance of freedom on Chelsea Embankment — Gissing keeps showing us characters who know what they believe and cannot live by it.
Which brings us, I think, to the heart of the novel — the collision between principle and desire, and what it costs to choose one over the other.

segments.title: Principle Versus Desire: The Novel's Central Debate

utterances.text: We've been exploring how Gissing uses atmosphere and isolation to press his characters toward impossible choices.
Now those choices become explicit — because at the heart of this novel is a debate that the characters themselves are conducting, fiercely, about principle and desire.
And the great thing about Gissing is that he lets both sides of that debate be genuinely compelling.
Rhoda Nunn's position — that women must mount a widespread revolt against sexual instinct — is not a figure of fun.
She means it with absolute, blazing sincerity, and you feel it.
She says — and I want to read this exactly as she says it —

"The necessity of the case demands what you call a strained ideal. I am seriously convinced that before the female sex can be raised from its low level there will have to be a widespread revolt against sexual instinct."
That word 'strained' is doing extraordinary work — she's conceding the charge in the very act of defending herself.
And then she reaches for Christianity — the ascetic ideal — as if to say: we have done this before, and it remade the world.
It is a magnificent piece of rhetoric, and Gissing knows it is rhetoric.
Because the novel immediately sets about testing whether Rhoda can actually live by her own programme.
And what we discover — in an interior passage of quite devastating honesty — is that the foundation of her position has a crack in it.
Gissing writes of her, in free indirect style:
"If only she had once been loved, like other women — if she had listened to an offer of devotion, and rejected it — her heart would be more securely at peace."
There it is — the quiet tragedy beneath the manifesto.
She does not simply wish to have been loved. She wishes to have refused love — to have exercised the power of rejection.
That is a very precise account of vanity and longing tangled together, and it does not diminish Rhoda — it deepens her.
I want to push on something Edmund just said, because I think the crack in Rhoda's foundation is not merely personal — it is structural.
Gissing tells us she worries that some people might think she 'made a virtue of necessity.'
And that anxiety is not trivial — it goes to the legitimacy of her entire social project.
A leader who has never been tempted cannot demonstrate that she has overcome temptation — only that she has been passed over by it.
Which is why the Barfoot plot is not a romantic digression — it is the novel's central experiment.
Gissing needs to put Rhoda in the crucible and see whether the ideal survives contact with a real, breathing, attractive man who actually wants her.
And the answer Gissing gives is genuinely uncomfortable — which is exactly right.
Because by the time we reach the crisis with Barfoot, Rhoda's principle and her desire have become almost indistinguishable from each other.
She cannot trust him, and she cannot let him go — and Gissing captures that bind in one extraordinary sentence.
"The incredulity she could not help must either part them for ever, or be to her an occasion of new triumph."
'An occasion of new triumph.' She's still doing it — still reaching for the language of victory, even while her heart is breaking.
That is a performer's detail — the way a character's habitual idiom betrays them under pressure.
I think one must observe, though, that Monica Madden represents the opposite experiment — and it is no less searching.
Monica does not hold a principle against desire — she is consumed by desire against the prison of her marriage.
And Gissing gives us the full moral weight of her situation in language that is almost juridical in its precision.

"It was dishonour to live with a man she could not love, whether her heart cherished another image or was merely vacant. A dishonour to which innumerable women submitted, a dishonour glorified by social precept, enforced under dread penalties."
Three uses of the word 'dishonour' in four lines — he hammers at it like a judge pronouncing sentence.
And yet the dishonour is 'glorified by social precept' — the very institution meant to confer honour has become its negation.
That is not a radical pamphlet speaking — that is a novelist of the first order seeing the institution of marriage whole.
Edmund is right that Gissing sees the institution whole — and I'd add that what he sees is the mechanism by which women are made to enforce their own subordination.
The 'dread penalties' Monica fears are not legal — they are social. They are the withdrawal of respectability.
And what makes Monica's passage to Bevis so devastating is that Gissing shows us the precise moment when she stops fighting that mechanism.
He writes:
"She saw something before her — something she durst not, even an hour ago, have steadily contemplated; it drew her with the force of fate."
'The force of fate' — that is not romance. That is a woman in a system that has exhausted her alternatives.
She is not choosing freely — she is choosing at the very edge of what the system has left her.
And yet — and I want to hold this alongside what Daniel's just said — Gissing also lets Monica articulate something that sounds almost like freedom.
There's a sentence in chapter twenty-two that stopped me cold when I first read it — one of those lines where a novel suddenly speaks its own secret aloud.
"The independence she had been struggling to assert ever since her marriage meant only freedom to love."
Eight words that unravel all of Rhoda's programme — and Monica doesn't even know she's doing it.
She has been fighting for independence, and the novel quietly reveals that her independence was always in the service of surrender.
Gissing doesn't judge her for that — he just watches it, with those clear, cold, sorrowful eyes of his.
Monica's collapse of independence into desire, and Rhoda's refusal to allow the same collapse — these are the novel's two poles, and neither survives the novel intact.
Which raises the question of what exactly does survive — and what Gissing means us to carry away from these lives that resist easy resolution.
That persistence — and the paradox at the centre of it — is what we'll turn to next.

segments.title: The Odd Women's Persistence and Paradox

utterances.text: We've been sitting with Gissing's central debate — principle against desire, ideology against longing.
What I want to explore now is what the novel leaves us with — its persistence, and its beautiful, unresolved paradoxes.
The paradox that haunts me most is one the novel earns through Monica's confession to Rhoda.
Monica isn't a villain for what she admits — she's the novel's most honest character.
She tells Rhoda exactly why she married Widdowson, and it's devastating in its clarity.
"I should never have married him if I hadn't been tempted by the thoughts of living easily — and I feared so — that I might always be alone."
That dash before 'that I might always be alone' — Gissing earns that pause.
It's not weakness she's describing — it's rational calculation under a system that gave women almost no other options.
The terror of her sisters' lives — the Maddens scratching along in poverty — is the material condition that makes Widdowson look like salvation.
I won't quarrel with that reading, though I'd frame it differently.
Monica's confession is a study in a failure of courage — and Gissing is entirely compassionate about it, which is what elevates the scene.
What the novel insists upon — and I think this is Gissing's moral centre — is that the examined life remains possible even after catastrophic choices.
Rhoda does not condemn Monica.
She offers her something far more demanding — a future.
And the language Rhoda uses to offer that future — I mean, it's extraordinary prose to speak aloud.
There's a passage where Rhoda sketches out this vision of Monica returned to the cause — and it has almost the quality of an incantation.
"We seemed to have lost you; but before long you will be one of us again.
I mean, you will be one of the women who are fighting in woman's cause.
You will prove by your life that we can be responsible human beings — trustworthy, conscious of purpose."
'Conscious of purpose' — I would give quite a lot to have written that phrase.
It doesn't ask Monica to be heroic — it asks her to be deliberate.
And that word 'trustworthy' — it's doing political work as much as moral work.
Rhoda is making an argument to the world, not just to Monica.
Which connects directly to what Mary Barfoot does earlier — that extraordinary lecture where she reads out the anonymous abusive letter from an unemployed clerk.
She doesn't suppress it or dismiss it — she reads it all the way through to her students.
Gissing tells us: "she read it all through... For all that, his uncivil attack had a meaning, and there were plenty of people ready to urge his argument in more respectable terms."
That move — taking the hostile argument seriously, more seriously than its author deserves — is Gissing's intellectual honesty at its sharpest.
The threat to women's employment is real, the economic grievance is real — and the novel won't let you look away from that.
Mary Barfoot is, I think, the novel's most undervalued figure.
She has a quality that Gissing admired and rarely achieved in his characters — she can hold two truths simultaneously without collapsing into either.
The clerk's resentment is base in expression — but not entirely base in fact.
Mary acknowledges this without surrendering an inch of her position.
That is, I would submit, a more difficult intellectual feat than most polemicists manage.
And there's the comedy of it too — which one mustn't miss.
The taste of this epistle was as bad as its grammar — Gissing gets a lovely dry joke in before the serious argument begins.
He knows perfectly well that a bitter anonymous letter is inherently comic — and he lets Mary know it too.
The laughter in the room — you can almost hear it — and then the pivot to genuine seriousness.
That's the mark of a brilliant speaker — and of a novelist who writes for the voice as much as for the page.
What I keep returning to — and this is what makes the novel persist — is Rhoda's injunction to Monica near the end of their exchange.
She's not offering comfort exactly — she's offering a demand dressed as encouragement.
She says to Monica — and I think this may be the moral core of the whole novel —
"Think bravely and nobly of yourself! Say to yourself: This and that it is in me to do, and I will do it!"
Not 'be good,' not 'be patient' — but 'think bravely.'
The mind as the instrument of liberation — that's the radical claim, and Gissing makes it quietly, through a woman speaking to a woman.
I find that I cannot improve upon Rhoda's formulation — which is perhaps the highest compliment one can pay a novelist.
'This and that it is in me to do' — the syntax itself is unusual, almost archaic, as though the idea requires a different grammar to contain it.
Gissing was not a systematic thinker, but in moments like this he was a genuine moralist.
He believed that self-knowledge was not a luxury but a necessity — and that it could be achieved even by those the world had treated badly.
The odd women of the title — the surplus women, statistically unclaimed — end up being anything but odd in the sense of marginal.
They're the ones asking the sharpest questions, bearing the full weight of the novel's intelligence.
Rhoda and Mary between them carry a vision that the twentieth century would spend decades catching up to.
And Gissing — bless him — doesn't tidy it up.
He lets the contradictions stand, the losses stand, the unanswered questions stand.
And perhaps that is precisely where the novel's persistence comes from — not from its answers but from the integrity of its questions.
We began today with a novel that refuses to be comfortable, and I think we've honoured that refusal.
My profound thanks to Daniel Rosen, whose eye for what the system costs its people never let us settle for easy readings.
To Sir Edmund Leigh, who reminded us that moral seriousness and literary pleasure are not in competition.
And to Oliver Trevelyan, who made us hear Gissing's prose the way it deserves to be heard — with relish, with care, and with just the right amount of mischief.
We've ranged today from Monica's terrified compromises to Rhoda's fierce demands, from Mary Barfoot's lectern to the novel's most unresolvable silences.
The Odd Women was published in 1893, and it reads, in the best possible sense, as if it is not finished with us yet.
Thank you for listening.

c14:p123.text:
“I haven’t to do with the subject at all,” Rhoda answered, with perhaps
a trace of impatience. “My work and thought are for the women who do
not marry—the “odd women” I call them. They alone interest me. One
mustn’t undertake too much.”
c14:p123.summary: Rhoda declares that marriage is not her concern, only the lives and independence of unmarried women.
c14:p123.best_quote: My work and thought are for the women who do not marry—the "odd women" I call them. They alone interest me. One mustn't undertake too much.

c13:p108.text:
“That is confusing the point at issue,” Rhoda exclaimed irritably.
“Have I ever denied the force of such feelings? My grief would have
blinded me to all larger considerations, of course. But she was happily
 not  my sister, and I remained free to speak the simple truth about
her case. It isn’t personal feeling that directs a great movement in
civilization. If you were right, I also was right. You should have
recognized the inevitable discord of our opinions at that moment.”
c13:p108.summary: Rhoda refuses to accept Mary's emotional argument, asserting that movements for change must not be governed by personal attachment, and that both women were logically consistent—hence the inevitable discord.
c13:p108.best_quote: It isn't personal feeling that directs a great movement in civilization. If you were right, I also was right. You should have recognized the inevitable discord of our opinions at that moment

c17:p124.text:
“To scorn the old idea that a woman’s life is wasted if she does not
marry. My work is to help those women who, by sheer necessity, must
live alone—women whom vulgar opinion ridicules. How can I help them so
effectually as by living among them, one of them, and showing that my
life is anything but weariness and lamentation? I am fitted for this.
It gives me a sense of power and usefulness which I enjoy. Your cousin
is doing the same work admirably. If I deserted I should despise
myself.”
c17:p124.summary: Rhoda articulates that her work is to help unmarried women by rejecting the notion that their lives are wasted, and by demonstrating through her own example that single life can be vital, meaningful, and powerful.
c17:p124.best_quote: To scorn the old idea that a woman's life is wasted if she does not marry. My work is to help those women who, by sheer necessity, must live alone—women whom vulgar opinion ridicules. How can I help them so effectually as by living among them, one of them, and showing that my life is anything but weariness and lamentation?

c4:p175.text:
“Something like that, they say. So many  odd  women—no making a pair
with them. The pessimists call them useless, lost, futile lives. I,
naturally—being one of them myself—take another view. I look upon
them as a great reserve. When one woman vanishes in matrimony, the
reserve offers a substitute for the world’s work. True, they are not
all trained yet—far from it. I want to help in that—to train the
reserve.”
c4:p175.summary: Rhoda explains that the surplus women—the 'odd women'—are viewed pessimistically as useless but she considers them a valuable reserve for necessary work, available to replace those lost to marriage.
c4:p175.best_quote: So many odd women—no making a pair with them. The pessimists call them useless, lost, futile lives. I, naturally—being one of them myself—take another view. I look upon them as a great reserve. When one woman vanishes in matrimony, the reserve offers a substitute for the world's work.

c8:p50.text:
“Yes,” he continued, “she was by birth a lady—which made the
infliction harder to bear. Poor old Poppleton! Again and again I have
heard him—what do you think?—laboriously  explaining  jests to her.
That was a trial, as you may imagine. There we sat, we three, in the
unbeautiful little parlour—for they were anything but rich. Poppleton
would say something that convulsed me with laughter—in spite of my
efforts, for I always dreaded the result so much that I strove my
hardest to do no more than smile appreciation. My laugh compelled Mrs.
Poppleton to stare at me—oh, her eyes! Thereupon, her husband began
his dread performance. The patience, the heroic patience, of that dear,
good fellow! I have known him explain, and re-explain, for a quarter of
an hour, and invariably without success. It might be a mere pun; Mrs.
Poppleton no more understood the nature of a pun than of the binomial
theorem. But worse was when the jest involved some allusion. When I
heard Poppleton begin to elucidate, to expound, the perspiration
already on his forehead, I looked at him with imploring anguish. Why
 would  he attempt the impossible? But the kind fellow couldn’t
disregard his wife’s request. Shall I ever forget her. “Oh—yes—I
see”?—when obviously she saw nothing but the wall at which she sat
staring.”
c8:p50.summary: Everard elaborates the torture of Poppleton's marriage through extended comic detail: his friend's endless, futile attempts to explain jokes to his wife's blank incomprehension, culminating in the image of her staring unseeing at the wall.
c8:p50.best_quote: Poor old Poppleton! Again and again I have heard him—what do you think?—laboriously explaining jests to her... I have known him explain, and re-explain, for a quarter of an hour, and invariably without success.

c15:p48.text:
Surely he was the easiest of men to live with. When he first became
aware that Monica suffered an occasional discontent, it caused him
troublous surprise. As soon as he understood that she desired more
freedom of movement, he became anxious, suspicious, irritable. Nothing
like a quarrel had yet taken place between them, but Widdowson began to
perceive that he must exert authority in a way he had imagined would
never be necessary. All his fears, after all, were not groundless.
Monica’s undomestic life, and perhaps the association with those
Chelsea people, had left results upon her mind. By way of mild
discipline, he first of all suggested a closer attention to the affairs
of the house. Would it not be well if she spent an hour a day in sewing
or fancy work? Monica so far obeyed as to provide herself with some
plain needlework, but Widdowson, watching with keen eye, soon remarked
that her use of the needle was only a feint. He lay awake o’ nights,
pondering darkly.
c15:p48.summary: When Widdowson detects Monica's discontent, he becomes suspicious and anxious, attributing her desire for freedom to her past work and Chelsea friends; he attempts mild discipline through household demands.
c15:p48.best_quote: Monica's undomestic life, and perhaps the association with those Chelsea people, had left results upon her mind. By way of mild discipline, he first of all suggested a closer attention to the affairs of the house.

c4:p85.text:
Her own future was more hopeful than theirs had ever been. She knew
herself good-looking. Men had followed her in the street and tried to
make her acquaintance. Some of the girls with whom she lived regarded
her enviously, spitefully. But had she really the least chance of
marrying a man whom she could respect—not to say love?
c4:p85.summary: Monica recognizes her beauty attracts men and envies from other girls, but doubts she has any real chance of marrying a respectable man.

c7:p165.text:
“I have behaved very imprudently,” continued the girl. But I don’t
see—I can’t see—what else I could have done. Things are so badly
arranged. It wasn’t possible for us to be introduced by any one who
knew us both, so I had either to break off your acquaintance after that
first conversation, or conduct myself as I have been doing. I think
it’s a very hard position. My sisters would call me an immodest girl,
but I don’t think it is true. I may perhaps come to feel you as a girl
ought to when she marries, and how else can I tell unless I meet you
and talk with you? And your position is just the same. I don’t blame
you for a moment; I think it would be ridiculous to blame you. Yet we
have gone against the ordinary rule, and people would make us suffer
for it—or me, at all events.
c7:p165.summary: Monica defends their unconventional conduct as necessary and expresses her hope that love might develop through acquaintance; she acknowledges the social penalty women face for such behavior.
c7:p165.best_quote: I may perhaps come to feel you as a girl ought to when she marries, and how else can I tell unless I meet you and talk with you? And your position is just the same. I don't blame you for a moment; I think it would be ridiculous to blame you. Yet we have gone against the ordinary rule, and people would make us suffer for it—or me, at all events.

c15:p53.text:
To-night, it being Sunday, he took down a volume of Barrow’s Sermons.
Though not strictly orthodox in religious faith, he conformed to the
practices of the Church of England, and since his marriage had been
more scrupulous on this point than before. He abhorred unorthodoxy in a
woman, and would not on any account have suffered Monica to surmise
that he had his doubts concerning any article of the Christian faith.
Like most men of his kind, he viewed religion as a precious and
powerful instrument for directing the female conscience. Frequently he
read aloud to his wife, but this evening he showed no intention of
doing so. Monica, however, sat unoccupied. After glancing at her once
or twice, he said reprovingly,—
c15:p53.summary: Widdowson, not strictly orthodox himself, reads Barrow's Sermons on Sunday and uses religion to constrain Monica's behaviour; he values faith primarily as an instrument of female control.
c15:p53.best_quote: Like most men of his kind, he viewed religion as a precious and powerful instrument for directing the female conscience.

c23:p1.text:
He had read somewhere that a persistently jealous husband may not
improbably end by irritating an innocent wife into affording real
ground for jealousy. A man with small knowledge of the world is much
impressed by dicta such as these; they get into the crannies of his
mind, and thence direct the course of his thinking. Widdowson, before
his marriage, had never suspected the difficulty of understanding a
woman; had he spoken his serious belief on that subject, it would have
been found to represent the most primitive male conception of the
feminine being. Women were very like children; it was rather a task to
amuse them and to keep them out of mischief. Therefore the blessedness
of household toil, in especial the blessedness of child-bearing and all
that followed. Intimacy with Monica had greatly affected his views, yet
chiefly by disturbing them; no firmer ground offered itself to his
treading when he perforce admitted that his former standpoint was
every day assailed by some incontestable piece of evidence. Woman had
individual characters; that discovery, though not a very profound one,
impressed him with the force of something arrived at by independent
observation. Monica often puzzled him gravely; he could not find the
key to her satisfactions and discontents. To regard her simply as a
human being was beyond the reach of his intelligence. He cast the blame
of his difficulties upon sex, and paid more attention to the hints on
such topics afforded him by his reading. He would endeavour to keep his
jealousy out of sight, lest the mysterious tendency of the female
nature might prompt Monica to deliberate wrongdoing.
c23:p1.summary: Gissing dissects Widdowson's primitive conception of womanhood, his shock at discovering Monica's individuality, and his misguided reliance on books to understand female nature.
c23:p1.best_quote: Women were very like children; it was rather a task to amuse them and to keep them out of mischief.

c19:p1.text:
Widdowson knew that Monica was going to the Academy. He allowed her to
set forth alone, and even tried to persuade himself that he was
indifferent as to the hour of her return; but she had not long been
gone before he followed. Insufferable misery possessed him. His married
life threatened to terminate in utter wreck, and he had the anguish of
recognizing that to a great extent this catastrophe would be his own
fault. Resolve as he might, he found it impossible to repress the
impulses of jealousy which, as soon as peace had been declared between
them, brought about a new misunderstanding. Terrible thoughts
smouldered in his mind; he felt himself to be one of those men who are
driven by passion into crime. Deliberately he had brooded over a tragic
close to the wretchedness of his existence; he would kill himself, and
Monica should perish with him. But an hour of contentment sufficed to
banish such visions as sheer frenzy. He saw once more how harmless, how
natural, were Monica’s demands, and how peacefully he might live with
her but for the curse of suspicion from which he could not free
himself. Any other man would deem her a model of wifely virtue. Her care
of the house was all that reason could desire. In her behaviour he had
never detected the slightest impropriety. He believed her chaste as any
woman living She asked only to be trusted, and that, in spite of all,
was beyond his power.
c19:p1.summary: Widdowson follows Monica to the Academy despite claiming indifference, consumed by jealousy and capable of violent fantasies, though he recognizes Monica's virtue.
c19:p1.best_quote: Terrible thoughts smouldered in his mind; he felt himself to be one of those men who are driven by passion into crime.

c19:p37.text:
“I have my faults; I know them only too well. One of them is that I
cannot bear you to make friends with people who are not of my kind. I
shall never be able to endure that.”
c19:p37.summary: Widdowson confesses that he cannot tolerate Monica's association with people of different social standing.
c19:p37.best_quote: I have my faults; I know them only too well. One of them is that I cannot bear you to make friends with people who are not of my kind.

c23:p35.text:
Suspicions thickened about him. He would have thought it utterly
impossible for Miss Madden to disgrace herself in this vulgar way, and
the appalling discovery affected his view of Monica. They were sisters;
they had characteristics in common, family traits, weaknesses. If the
elder woman could fall into this degradation, might there not be
possibilities in Monica’s character such as he had refused to
contemplate? Was there not terrible reason for mistrusting her? What
did she mean by her message to Virginia?
c23:p35.summary: Widdowson's discovery of Virginia's drinking causes him to imagine similar vulnerabilities in Monica, and he grows suspicious of her mysterious message.
c23:p35.best_quote: They were sisters; they had characteristics in common, family traits, weaknesses. If the elder woman could fall into this degradation, might there not be possibilities in Monica's character such as he had refused to contemplate?

c24:p91.text:
Without another word he departed. But went only a short distance, and
until midnight kept Mrs. Conisbee’s door in view. The rain fell, the
air was raw; shelterless, and often shivering with fever, Widdowson
walked the pavement with a constable’s regularity. He could not but
remember the many nights when he thus kept watch in Walworth Road and
in Rutland Street, with jealousy, then too, burning in his heart, but
also with amorous ardours, never again to be revived. A little more
than twelve months ago! And he had waited, longed for marriage through
half a lifetime.
c24:p91.summary: Widdowson keeps watch outside Mrs. Conisbee's house through the night, remembering his earlier jealous vigils and his long-awaited, now-destroyed marriage.
c24:p91.best_quote: A little more than twelve months ago! And he had waited, longed for marriage through half a lifetime.

c19:p55.text:
Monica could not reply. That word “love” had grown a weariness to her
upon his lips. She did not love him; could not pretend to love him.
Every day the distance between them widened, and when he took her in
his arms she had to struggle with a sense of shrinking, of disgust. The
union was unnatural; she felt herself constrained by a hateful force
when he called upon her for the show of wifely tenderness. Yet how was
she to utter this? The moment such a truth had passed her lips she must
leave him. To declare that no trace of love remained in her heart, and
still to live with him—that was impossible! The dark foresight of a
necessity of parting from him corresponded in her to those lurid
visions which at times shook Widdowson with a horrible temptation.
c19:p55.summary: Monica cannot reply because she realizes she no longer loves him; physical contact causes her revulsion, and she foresees inevitable separation as the only honest course.
c19:p55.best_quote: Every day the distance between them widened, and when he took her in his arms she had to struggle with a sense of shrinking, of disgust.

c24:p46.text:
She clung upon his arms and strove to raise herself. The bloodless
lips, the choked voice, meant dread of him, but the distortion of her
features was hatred and the will to resist.
c24:p46.summary: Monica clings to Widdowson's arms, showing fear but also hatred and resistance.
c24:p46.best_quote: The bloodless lips, the choked voice, meant dread of him, but the distortion of her features was hatred and the will to resist.

c8:p18.text:
He had a tall, muscular frame, and a head of striking outline, with
large nose, full lips, deep-set eyes, and prominent eyebrows. His hair
was the richest tone of chestnut; his moustache and beard—the latter
peaking slightly forward—inclined to redness. Excellent health
manifested itself in the warm purity of his skin, in his cheerful
aspect, and the lightness of his bearing. The lower half of his
forehead was wrinkled, and when he did not fix his look on anything in
particular, his eyelids drooped, giving him for the moment an air of
languor. On sitting down, he at once abandoned himself to a posture of
the completest ease, which his admirable proportions made graceful.
From his appearance one would have expected him to speak in rather loud
and decided tones; but he had a soft voice, and used it with all the
discretion of good breeding, so that at times it seemed to caress the
ear. To this mode of utterance corresponded his smile, which was
frequent, but restrained to the expression of a delicate, good-natured
irony.
c8:p18.summary: Gissing provides a detailed physical description of Everard: tall, muscular, striking features, rich chestnut hair, healthy appearance, but with wrinkled brow and drooping eyelids when relaxed; he moves with ease and speaks with soft, discrete grace.
c8:p18.best_quote: From his appearance one would have expected him to speak in rather loud and decided tones; but he had a soft voice, and used it with all the discretion of good breeding, so that at times it seemed to caress the ear.

c22:p190.text:
Monica listened, but with half-attention, her look fixed on the floor.
Encouraged by her silence, the lover went on in a strain of heightening
enthusiasm, depicting the raptures of their retirement from the world
in some suburb of Bordeaux. How this retreat was to escape the notice
of his business companions, through whom the scandal might get wind, he
did not suggest. The truth was, Bevis found himself in an extremely
awkward position, with issues he had not contemplated, and all he cared
for was to avert the immediate peril of public discovery. The
easy-going, kindly fellow had never considered all the responsibility
involved in making mild love—timorously selfish from the first—to a
married woman who took his advances with desperate seriousness. He had
not in him the stuff of vigorous rascality, still less the only other
quality which can support a man in such a situation as this—heroism of
moral revolt. So he cut a very poor figure, and was dolefully aware of
it. He talked, talked; trying to disguise his feebleness in tinsel
phrases; and Monica still kept her eyes cast down.
c22:p190.summary: The narrator provides extended psychological analysis of Everard's character, showing he lacks both the capacity for bold villainy and the courage for moral heroism. He is aware of his own inadequacy even as he attempts to mask it with rhetoric.
c22:p190.best_quote: He had not in him the stuff of vigorous rascality, still less the only other quality which can support a man in such a situation as this—heroism of moral revolt. So he cut a very poor figure, and was dolefully aware of it.

c13:p122.text:
“Now see why. Womanly and womanish are two very different words; but
the latter, as the world uses it, has become practically synonymous
with the former. A womanly occupation means, practically, an occupation
that a man disdains. And here is the root of the matter. I repeat that
I am not first of all anxious to keep you supplied with daily bread. I
am a troublesome, aggressive, revolutionary person. I want to do away
with that common confusion of the words womanly and womanish, and I see
very clearly that this can only be effected by an armed movement, an
invasion by women of the spheres which men have always forbidden us to
enter. I am strenuously opposed to that view of us set forth in such
charming language by Mr. Ruskin—for it tells on the side of those men
who think and speak of us in a way the reverse of charming. Were we
living in an ideal world, I think women would not go to sit all day in
offices. But the fact is that we live in a world as far from ideal as
can be conceived. We live in a time of warfare, of revolt. If woman is
no longer to be womanish, but a human being of powers and
responsibilities, she must become militant, defiant. She must push her
claims to the extremity.
c13:p122.summary: Mary launches a sustained attack on Ruskin and conventional femininity, arguing that only militant assertion of women's right to work across all fields can advance civilization.
c13:p122.best_quote: I am a troublesome, aggressive, revolutionary person... women must become militant, defiant. She must push her claims to the extremity

c21:p0.text:
Mary Barfoot had never suffered from lack of interest in life. Many a
vivid moment dwelt in her memory; joys and sorrows, personal or of
larger scope, affected her the more deeply because of that ruling
intelligence which enabled her to transmute them into principles. No
longer anticipating or desiring any great change in her own
environment, in the modes and motives of her activity, she found it a
sufficient happiness to watch, and when possible to direct, the
tendency of younger lives. So kindly had nature tempered her
disposition, that already she had been able to outlive those fervours
of instinct which often make the middle life of an unwedded woman one
long repining; but her womanly sympathies remained. And at present
there was going forward under her own roof, within her daily
observation, a comedy, a drama, which had power to excite all her
disinterested emotions. It had been in progress for twelve months, and
now, unless she was strangely mistaken, the  denouement  drew very near.
c21:p0.summary: Mary Barfoot reflects on her fulfilling life and observes a developing emotional drama between younger people in her household, sensing its climax approaches.

c25:p0.text:
Rhoda’s week at the seashore was spoilt by uncertain weather. Only two
days of abiding sunshine; for the rest, mere fitful gleams across a sky
heaped with stormclouds. Over Wastdale hung a black canopy; from
Scawfell came mutterings of thunder; and on the last night of the
week—when Monica fled from her home in pelting rain—tempest broke
upon the mountains and the sea. Wakeful until early morning, and at
times watching the sky from her inland-looking window, Rhoda saw the
rocky heights that frown upon Wastwater illuminated by lightning-flare
of such intensity and duration that miles of distance were annihilated,
and it seemed but a step to those stern crags and precipices.
c25:p0.summary: Rhoda's seaside holiday is marred by bad weather, with dramatic storms illuminating the landscape while Monica flees her home in rain.
c25:p0.best_quote: tempest broke upon the mountains and the sea

c27:p11.text:
Rhoda smiled a little, conscious of the extreme curiosity her friend
must be feeling, and determined not to gratify it. For by this time,
though her sunken cheeks were hard to reconcile with the enjoyment of a
summer holiday, she had matured a resolve to betray nothing of what she
had gone through. Her state of mind resembled that of the ascetic who
has arrived at a morbid delight in self-torture. She regarded the world
with an intense bitterness, and persuaded herself not only that the
thought of Everard Barfoot was hateful to her soul, but that sexual
love had become, and would ever be, to her an impure idea, a vice of
blood.
c27:p11.summary: Rhoda deliberately conceals her suffering from Miss Barfoot and embraces a morbid asceticism, persuading herself that Everard is hateful and that sexual love itself is impure.
c27:p11.best_quote: She regarded the world with an intense bitterness, and persuaded herself not only that the thought of Everard Barfoot was hateful to her soul, but that sexual love had become, and would ever be, to her an impure idea, a vice of blood.

c29:p1.text:
A fear of death compassed her about. Night after night it had thus
haunted her. In the daytime she could think of death with resignation,
as a refuge from miseries of which she saw no other end; but this hour
of silent darkness shook her with terrors. Reason availed nothing; its
exercise seemed criminal. The old faiths, never abandoned, though
modified by the breath of intellectual freedom that had just touched
her, reasserted all their power. She saw herself as a wicked woman, in
the eye of truth not less wicked than her husband declared her. A
sinner stubborn in impenitence, defending herself by a paltry ambiguity
that had all the evil of a direct lie. Her soul trembled in its
nakedness.
c29:p1.summary: Monica experiences a crisis of conscience, feeling herself a sinner despite intellectual reservations, with religious fears overwhelming her reason.
c29:p1.best_quote: Her soul trembled in its nakedness.

c29:p46.text:
She took train to York Road Station, and thence, as the night was fine,
walked to Chelsea. This semblance of freedom, together with the sense
of having taken a courageous resolve, raised her spirits. She hoped
that a detective might be tracking her; the futility of such measures
afforded her a contemptuous satisfaction. Not to arrive before the
appointed hour she loitered on Chelsea Embankment, and it gave her
pleasure to reflect that in doing this she was outraging the
proprieties. Her mind was in a strange tumult of rebellious and
distrustful thought. She had determined on making a confession to
Rhoda; but would she benefit by it? Was Rhoda generous enough to
appreciate her motives? It did not matter much. She would have
discharged a duty at the expense of such shame, and this fact alone
might strengthen her to face the miseries beyond.
c29:p46.summary: Monica travels by train to Chelsea, enjoying the illusion of freedom and the prospect of outwitting any detectives; her mind is tumultuous with rebellious thought and doubt about Rhoda's generosity.
c29:p46.best_quote: This semblance of freedom, together with the sense of having taken a courageous resolve, raised her spirits.

c6:p126.text:
“Surely that’s an unfortunate comparison,” said Rhoda coldly. “What man
lives in celibacy? Consider that unmentionable fact, and then say
whether I am wrong in refusing to forgive Miss Royston. Women’s battle
is not only against themselves. The necessity of the case demands what
you call a strained ideal. I am seriously convinced that before the
female sex can be raised from its low level there will have to be a
widespread revolt against sexual instinct. Christianity couldn’t spread
over the world without help of the ascetic ideal, and this great
movement for woman’s emancipation must also have its ascetics.”
c6:p126.summary: Rhoda rejects Barfoot's comparison, pointing out that men escape celibacy through sexual access; she insists that female emancipation requires ascetic resistance to sexual instinct, framing it as necessary as Christianity's ascetic ideal.
c6:p126.best_quote: The necessity of the case demands what you call a strained ideal. I am seriously convinced that before the female sex can be raised from its low level there will have to be a widespread revolt against sexual instinct.

c14:p139.text:
No man had ever made love to her; no man, to her knowledge, had ever
been tempted to do so. In certain moods she derived satisfaction from
this thought, using it to strengthen her life’s purpose; having passed
her thirtieth year, she might take it as a settled thing that she would
never be sought in marriage, and so could shut the doors on every
instinct tending to trouble her intellectual decisions. But these
instincts sometimes refused to be thus treated. As Miss Barfoot told
her, she was very young for her years, young in physique, young in
emotion. As a girl she had dreamt passionately, and the fires of her
nature, though hidden beneath aggregations of moral and mental
attainment, were not yet smothered. An hour of lassitude filled her
with despondency, none the less real because she was ashamed of it. If
only she had once been loved, like other women—if she had listened to
an offer of devotion, and rejected it—her heart would be more securely
at peace. So she thought. Secretly she deemed it a hard thing never to
have known that common triumph of her sex. And, moreover, it took away
from the merit of her position as a leader and encourager of women
living independently. There might be some who said, or thought, that
she made a virtue of necessity.
c14:p139.summary: Rhoda's interior monologue reveals her suppressed desire to have been loved and her anxiety that her celibacy might be seen as forced rather than chosen.
c14:p139.best_quote: If only she had once been loved, like other women—if she had listened to an offer of devotion, and rejected it—her heart would be more securely at peace. So she thought. Secretly she deemed it a hard thing never to have known that common triumph of her sex.

c26:p94.text:
The words fell upon her heart like a crushing weight. But she could not
yield. Last night she had suffered in his opinion by urging what he
thought a weak, womanly scruple; she had condescended to plead tenderly
with him, and had won her cause. Now she would prevail in another way.
If he were telling the truth, he should acknowledge that natural
suspicion made it incumbent upon him to clear so strange a case of its
difficulties. If he were guilty of deception, as she still believed,
though willing to admit to herself that Monica might be most at fault,
that there might have been no actual wrongdoing between them—he should
confess with humblest penitence, and beseech pardon. Impossible to take
any other attitude. Impossible to marry him with this doubt in her
mind—equally out of the question to seek Monica, and humiliate herself
by making inquiries on such a subject. Guilty or not, Monica would
regard her with secret disdain, with woman’s malice. Were she  able  to
believe him, that indeed would be a grand consummation of their love,
an ideal union of heart and soul. Listening to him, she had tried to
put faith in his indignant words. But it was useless. The incredulity
she could not help must either part them for ever, or be to her an
occasion of new triumph.
c26:p94.summary: Rhoda is devastated by Everard's threat to end the engagement but cannot overcome her suspicion. She reflects that she faces an impossible choice: either marry with doubt in her mind (which is unthinkable), or let him leave (which would shatter her). She considers whether Monica might be responsible, whether she could seek clarification, and realizes that any such approach would only humiliate her further.
c26:p94.best_quote: Listening to him, she had tried to put faith in his indignant words. But it was useless. The incredulity she could not help must either part them for ever, or be to her an occasion of new triumph.

c19:p73.text:
A husband’s misdirected jealousy excites in the wife derision and a
sense of superiority; more often than not, it fosters an unsuspected
attachment, prompts to a perverse pleasure in misleading. Monica became
aware of this; in her hours of misery she now and then gave a harsh
laugh, the result of thoughts not seriously entertained, but tempting
the fancy to recklessness. What, she asked herself again, would be the
end of it all? Ten years hence, would she have subdued her soul to a
life of weary insignificance, if not of dishonour? For it was dishonour
to live with a man she could not love, whether her heart cherished
another image or was merely vacant. A dishonour to which innumerable
women submitted, a dishonour glorified by social precept, enforced
under dread penalties.
c19:p73.summary: Monica's existential crisis crystallizes: to live loveless with Widdowson is dishonor, yet this dishonor is the fate of countless women, sanctioned by society and enforced by social penalties.
c19:p73.best_quote: What, she asked herself again, would be the end of it all? Ten years hence, would she have subdued her soul to a life of weary insignificance, if not of dishonour? For it was dishonour to live with a man she could not love, whether her heart cherished another image or was merely vacant. A dishonour to which innumerable women submitted, a dishonour glorified by social precept, enforced under dread penalties.

c22:p35.text:
She scarcely knew what words fell from her lips. Let him propose, let
him do what he liked; to her it was indifferent. She saw something
before her—something she durst not, even an hour ago, have steadily
contemplated; it drew her with the force of fate.
c22:p35.summary: Monica is absorbed in a vision of the future—meeting with Bevis—that she now faces with fatalistic acceptance.
c22:p35.best_quote: She saw something before her—something she durst not, even an hour ago, have steadily contemplated; it drew her with the force of fate.

c22:p1.text:
Tremor of self-consciousness kept Monica in dread of being watched and
suspected. Few people were present to-day, and after exchanging formal
words with Bevis, she moved away to talk with the hostess. Not till
half an hour had passed did she venture to obey the glances which her
all but avowed lover cast towards her in conversation. He was so much
at ease, so like what she had always known him, that Monica asked
herself whether she had not mistaken the meaning of his homage. One
moment she hoped it might be so; the next, she longed for some sign of
passionate devotion, and thought with anguish of the day, now so near,
when he would be gone for ever. This, she ardently believed, was the
man who should have been her husband. Him she could love with heart and
soul, could make his will her absolute law, could live on his smiles,
could devote herself to his interests. The independence she had been
struggling to assert ever since her marriage meant only freedom to
love. If she had understood herself as she now did, her life would
never have been thus cast into bondage.
c22:p1.summary: Monica's self-consciousness masks her longing for Bevis, whom she believes she truly loves and could devote herself to completely, unlike her constrained marriage.
c22:p1.best_quote: The independence she had been struggling to assert ever since her marriage meant only freedom to love.

c29:p149.text:
“Oh, if you could give me some of  your  strength! I have never been
able to look at life as you do. I should never have married him if I
hadn’t been tempted by the thoughts of living easily—and I feared
so—that I might always be alone—My sisters are so miserable; it
terrified me to think of struggling on through life as they do—”
